title: Anointing of Saul
overview: 1 Samuel 10 narrates the divine selection and anointing of Saul as the first king of Israel. The chapter details Samuel’s prophetic instructions to Saul, the miraculous signs confirming God’s choice, and Saul’s transformation by the Spirit of the Lord. It culminates in Saul’s public presentation before Israel, where he is chosen by lot and acclaimed as king despite some initial skepticism. This chapter marks a pivotal moment in Israel’s history, transitioning from the era of judges to monarchy, emphasizing God’s sovereign guidance in appointing leaders and the spiritual empowerment that accompanies divine calling.
structure:
**Verses 1-9: Samuel Anoints Saul and Gives Signs.** Samuel anoints Saul with oil, symbolizing God’s appointment as leader. He then gives Saul specific prophetic signs to confirm God’s choice, including encounters with men and prophets, and promises the Spirit of the Lord will transform him.

**Verses 10-13: Saul Prophesies Among the Prophets.** Saul meets a company of prophets and is filled with the Spirit, prophesying and demonstrating a visible change, which astonishes those who knew him, leading to the proverb about Saul among the prophets.

**Verses 14-16: Saul’s Disappearance and Inquiry.** After the prophetic encounter, Saul’s uncle questions him about their journey. When Saul cannot be found during the tribal selection, the people inquire of the Lord, who reveals Saul’s hiding place.

**Verses 17-24: Public Selection of Saul as King.** Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpeh, recounts God’s deliverance, rebukes their demand for a king as rejection of God, and leads the casting of lots to choose Saul, who is then publicly acclaimed as king.

**Verses 25-27: Samuel’s Instructions and Opposition to Saul.** Samuel explains the kingdom’s regulations and sends the people home. Saul returns to Gibeah with followers whose hearts God has touched, but some reject and despise him, doubting his ability to save Israel.

keyVerses.text: Then Samuel took a vial of oil, and poured it upon his head, and kissed him, and said, Is it not because the LORD hath anointed thee to be captain over his inheritance?
keyVerses.significance: This verse introduces the anointing of Saul, marking God’s sovereign choice and setting Saul apart as leader over Israel, symbolizing divine authority and blessing.

keyVerses.text: And the Spirit of the LORD will come upon thee, and thou shalt prophesy with them, and shalt be turned into another man.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the transformative power of the Spirit of the Lord, enabling Saul to fulfill his calling and demonstrating that true leadership depends on God’s empowerment.

keyVerses.text: And ye have this day rejected your God, who himself saved you out of all your adversities and your tribulations; and ye have said unto him, Nay, but set a king over us. Now therefore present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes, and by your thousands.
keyVerses.significance: Samuel rebukes Israel for rejecting God’s direct rule by demanding a human king, underscoring the tension between divine sovereignty and human governance.

keyVerses.text: And Samuel said to all the people, See ye him whom the LORD hath chosen, that there is none like him among all the people? And all the people shouted, and said, God save the king.
keyVerses.significance: This public acclamation affirms God’s choice of Saul as king, uniting the nation under divinely appointed leadership and inaugurating the monarchy.

characters.name: Saul
characters.description: The first king of Israel, anointed by Samuel and empowered by the Spirit of the Lord. Saul’s journey in this chapter shows his divine selection, spiritual transformation, and initial acceptance by the people despite some opposition.

characters.name: Samuel
characters.description: The prophet and judge who anoints Saul as king, provides prophetic signs, gathers Israel for the selection, and instructs the people on the kingdom’s manner. Samuel serves as God’s messenger and leader during this transitional period.

characters.name: The Spirit of the LORD
characters.description: God’s empowering presence that comes upon Saul, enabling him to prophesy and be transformed. The Spirit’s work confirms Saul’s divine appointment and equips him for leadership.

characters.name: Israelite People
characters.description: The nation of Israel who demand a king to lead them like other nations. They participate in the selection of Saul by lot, publicly acclaim him, but also include skeptics who doubt his ability to save them.

themes.description: The chapter emphasizes that kingship in Israel is not a human invention but ordained by God, who anoints and empowers the chosen leader, underscoring God’s control over political authority.

themes.theme: The Role of the Holy Spirit
themes.description: The Spirit of the Lord’s coming upon Saul signifies God’s enabling power for leadership and prophecy, illustrating the necessity of divine empowerment for fulfilling God’s purposes.
Israel’s demand for a king represents a rejection of God’s direct rule, highlighting the tension between trusting God’s sovereignty and seeking human solutions to governance.
Saul’s prophetic experience among the prophets serves as a sign of God’s approval and transformation, showing prophecy as a divine confirmation of leadership.

historicalContext: This chapter is set during the late period of the Judges, approximately the 11th century BC, a time when Israel was a loose confederation of tribes without centralized monarchy. The political landscape was unstable, with frequent threats from surrounding nations like the Philistines. The demand for a king reflects Israel’s desire to be like neighboring nations, moving from tribal leadership to monarchy. Geographically, the events occur in the territory of Benjamin and key locations such as Mizpeh and Gilgal, central sites for Israelite worship and assembly. The cultural context includes prophetic activity and the anointing ritual with oil, symbolizing divine selection and empowerment.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes God’s sovereign election in Saul’s anointing, viewing the Spirit’s empowerment as essential for godly leadership. The demand for a king is seen as a rejection of God’s kingship, yet God graciously provides a human king within His sovereign plan.

Dispensationalists interpret Saul’s anointing as part of God’s progressive revelation and kingdom program, with the Spirit’s coming marking a new dispensation of monarchy. They highlight the prophetic signs as God’s confirmation of Saul’s role in His unfolding plan.

Early Church Fathers often saw Saul’s anointing as a type of Christ’s kingship, with the Spirit’s coming prefiguring the Holy Spirit’s work in the Messiah. They also reflected on Israel’s rejection of God’s direct rule as a lesson on human sinfulness and the need for divine grace.

crossReferences.connection: This psalm speaks of God’s anointed king, paralleling Saul’s anointing as God’s chosen ruler over Israel.
The Spirit of the Lord coming upon a chosen one to empower and transform echoes the Spirit’s coming upon Saul in 1 Samuel 10.
Peter’s sermon about Jesus being anointed with the Holy Spirit parallels Saul’s anointing and Spirit empowerment for leadership.
God’s instructions regarding kingship in Israel provide the background for understanding the significance of Saul’s selection as king.
The promise of a righteous Branch from David’s line contrasts with Saul’s imperfect kingship but affirms God’s ultimate plan for a divinely appointed king.

application: Trust God’s sovereign choice in leadership rather than relying solely on human wisdom or popular demand.
Seek the empowering presence of the Holy Spirit to fulfill God’s calling in your life.
Recognize the importance of obedience to God’s instructions even when circumstances are uncertain.
Be open to God’s transformative work that changes your heart and character for His purposes.
Support godly leaders through prayer and encouragement, understanding their need for divine guidance.
Avoid rejecting God’s direct rule in your life by submitting to His authority rather than human substitutes.
conclusion: 1 Samuel 10 stands as a foundational chapter marking Israel’s transition to monarchy under God’s sovereign guidance. It reveals the divine initiative in appointing leaders, the necessity of the Spirit’s empowerment, and the tension between human desires and God’s perfect rule. For believers today, it underscores the importance of trusting God’s choices, seeking His Spirit’s transforming power, and submitting to His authority in all areas of life. Saul’s anointing invites reflection on God’s providence and the call to faithful obedience amid change.
timeline: c. 1050 BC - Establishment of the Monarchy in Israel

definitions.definition: To be ceremonially consecrated by the pouring of oil, signifying God’s selection and empowerment for a specific role or office.
To speak forth God’s message under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, often involving foretelling or forth-telling divine truth.
A small container or bottle, here used to hold the oil for anointing.
A leader or chief officer; in this context, one appointed by God to lead His inheritance, Israel.
A term meaning worthless or wicked persons; here referring to those who opposed Saul and despised him.

outline.heading: Samuel Anoints Saul and Gives Signs

outline.heading: Saul Prophesies and Is Transformed
outline.description: The Spirit of the Lord comes upon Saul, enabling him to prophesy among other prophets, demonstrating his transformation and God’s empowerment.

outline.heading: Saul’s Disappearance and Divine Inquiry
outline.description: Saul’s uncle questions him, and when Saul cannot be found during the tribal selection, the people seek the Lord’s guidance to locate him.

outline.heading: Public Selection and Acclamation of Saul
outline.description: Samuel gathers Israel, recounts God’s deliverance, rebukes their demand for a king, and leads the casting of lots to choose Saul, who is then publicly acclaimed.

outline.description: Samuel explains the kingdom’s regulations, sends the people home, and Saul returns to Gibeah, where some reject him despite God touching the hearts of his followers.
